ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 3 — Sick Visit — Martin Luther

code.originalText: Same-day sick visit for right flank pain

text.paragraph: Severe right flank pain since early this morning. [S]

Professor Luther came in the same morning. He woke at about four with severe, colicky pain in the right flank that comes in waves and spreads to the right groin and testicle. He has felt sick and vomited once, and he has a constant urge to pass urine, passing small amounts. No fever or chills. He says it is the same pain as the stone he passed last year. He started hydrochlorothiazide and sertraline two weeks ago, increasing sertraline to 50 mg a week ago, and has used meclizine once this month. He has had no vertigo attack since the last visit, and his mood is no worse; he has no thoughts of harming himself. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 2026-08-25; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Restless, moving to find a position; temperature 36.9 C; blood pressure 142/88, pulse 96
Soft; mild right lower quadrant tenderness without guarding; no masses; no pulsatile mass
Testes normal, no tenderness or swelling

Recurrent attacks of spinning vertigo for about three months, the worst twelve days ago, lasting hours, with roaring tinnitus, fullness and muffled hearing in the left ear and nausea, the tinnitus persisting between attacks; with low mood, poor sleep and loss of interest; cause not established at intake: an inner-ear disorder suspected, with vestibular migraine, vestibular schwannoma and posterior circulation stroke to be excluded and depression to be assessed; otology consultation requested
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to his documented attacks of April and July 1527; superseded by the diagnoses at the second visit.

Ménière disease of the left ear, definite (AAO-HNS 2020 and Bárány Society criteria), with low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss and persistent tinnitus in the left ear; vestibular migraine considered and judged unlikely as the main cause; vestibular schwannoma excluded by MRI
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at the otology consultation, linked to his documented attacks and to the retrospective diagnosis of Ménière disease (R).

Major depressive disorder, recurrent, moderate (DSM-5-TR), with low mood, poor sleep, loss of interest, guilt and fatigue for about two months, after earlier periods of spiritual crisis and low mood; no suicidal ideation
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis linked to his documented Anfechtungen and low periods; not a claim that he was so diagnosed; the retrospective psychiatric readings are disputed (R).
Urinary stone disease: one stone passed spontaneously last year after severe pain; stone type and metabolic risk not yet known at intake
S — Synthetic modern problem anchored to his documented first stone in 1526.

Right distal ureteral stone, 5 mm, at the ureterovesical junction, with mild right hydronephrosis and renal colic; no infection; kidney function normal; managed with naproxen and tamsulosin; passed nine days later; resolved
S — Synthetic acute problem anchored to his documented recurrent stones; this episode is not a historical claim.

list.item:
Right distal ureteral stone with renal colic (N20.1). Colicky flank-to-groin pain, 30 red cells per high-power field and a known stone history fit renal colic. Low-dose CT shows a 5 mm stone at the right ureterovesical junction with mild hydronephrosis and no other stones. White cells 9.8 x10^3/uL, no fever, and no infection on the urine, so this is uncomplicated. Creatinine 1.12 mg/dL and eGFR above 60 are normal. The non-fasting glucose of 108 mg/dL reflects pain and will be rechecked. A stone of this size in the distal ureter usually passes within weeks; tamsulosin raises the chance under the AUA guideline. Naproxen controls the pain; a short course is acceptable with normal kidney function, taken with food because sertraline adds a little to the bleeding risk. The thiazide does not cause stones and may help prevent calcium stones. [S]
Naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food for up to 7 days; acetaminophen for extra pain; no opioid needed.
Tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily until the stone passes, for up to four weeks; may cause light-headedness on standing, so rise slowly, which also matters with his vertigo.
Strain all urine and bring any stone for analysis.
Drink normally; extra fluid does not speed passage.
Go to an emergency department for fever, uncontrolled pain or vomiting, or no urine.
If the stone has not passed in four weeks, urology referral for removal.
Continue hydrochlorothiazide and sertraline.

Ménière disease of the left ear (H81.02). No attacks since the consultation. [S]
No change.

Recurrent depression (F33.1). Early on sertraline; no suicidal thoughts. [S]
Safety plan unchanged; 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and the clinic number confirmed.

text.paragraph: Guideline basis: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline (2014); Surgical Management of Stones: American Urological Association/Endourological Society Guideline, Part I (2016)
Follow-up: Telephone check in two days. Preventive visit in two weeks. Six-week review as booked, with renal ultrasound. Next scheduled visit 2026-09-08: periodic adult preventive visit. [S]
